subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Find the angle between the curves y² = 4x and x² + y² = 5.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IB (2026-27 edition), book p.217, chapter 10 APPLICATIONS OF DERIVATIVES, the TANGENTS AND NORMALS sub-section, Short Answer question 5(i). recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — say how you find where the curves meet, which root you reject and why, and what formula gives the angle.

steps.label: Find the point of intersection
steps.margin_note: Two marks, and the two most often lost. Substitute y² = 4x into the circle so only x is left. The root x = −5 has to be rejected in writing, not silently — y² = 4x forces x ≥ 0.
lines: Given curves:  y² = 4x   …(i)   and   x² + y² = 5   …(ii)
From (i), y² = 4x ≥ 0, so x cannot be negative. Reject x = −5.
∴ the curves meet at P(1, 2) and at (1, −2). Work at P(1, 2).

recall.must_convey: That substituting y² = 4x into the circle gives x² + 4x − 5 = 0, x = 1 (rejecting x = −5), so the point is (1, 2).

steps.why: The angle between two curves is the angle between their tangents at a point they share, so nothing can be differentiated usefully until that point is known. Rejecting x = −5 with a stated reason is part of the method mark.
common_mistakes: Keeping x = −5 and producing a second angle at a point that does not exist.
Rejecting x = −5 silently, without writing the reason y² = 4x ≥ 0.
steps.memory_tip: Substitute whichever square is already isolated — here y² is given free, so it goes straight into the circle. Putting x = y²/4 into the circle also works and gives y⁴ + 16y² − 80 = 0, with the same points.

steps.label: Find both slopes there
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Differentiate each curve implicitly and substitute the point AFTER differentiating. Label the two slopes m₁ and m₂ so the next line is easy to read.

recall.must_convey: That m₁ = 2/y = 1 for the parabola and m₂ = −x/y = −1/2 for the circle at (1, 2).

steps.why: Both curves pass through the same point, but each has its own tangent there. Two separate derivatives, each evaluated at the same point, is what the angle formula needs.
common_mistakes: Substituting the point into the curve before differentiating, which leaves a number with no derivative.
Writing the circle slope as x/y and losing the minus sign.
Using the point (1, −2) for one slope and (1, 2) for the other.
steps.memory_tip: For x² + y² = r² the slope is always −x/y, because the tangent is perpendicular to the radius.

steps.label: Apply the angle formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The modulus keeps the acute angle, which is the one asked for. Give the exact form Tan⁻¹3 and the degree value beside it.
lines: If θ is the angle between the curves at P, then

recall.must_convey: That tanθ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)| = 3, so θ = Tan⁻¹3.

steps.why: The angle between two curves is defined as the angle between their tangents, and the tangent-of-difference formula for two straight lines applies directly once both slopes are known.
common_mistakes: Writing 1 − m₁m₂ in the denominator instead of 1 + m₁m₂.
Dropping the modulus and reporting a negative tangent value.
Leaving the answer as tanθ = 3 without stating θ = Tan⁻¹3.
steps.memory_tip: Difference on top, one plus the product underneath — the same formula as the angle between two straight lines.

insider_note: y² = 4x forces x ≥ 0, so the root x = −5 is rejected immediately. Both intersection points share x = 1, with y = ±2.
